A policy specifies how observations or states determine actions.
Its mathematical form, training objective, data collection, and deployment updates answer different questions.
Keeping those questions together helps distinguish imitation and reinforcement learning from the timing of computation.

## Policy and learning objective {#policies}

A stochastic policy $\pi(a\mid o)$ gives a distribution over actions given observations.
A deterministic policy gives a particular action or chunk, such as $a=f_\theta(o)$.
Sampling from a distribution and selecting its most likely action are different decision rules.

Behavioural cloning fits a policy to demonstrated actions with supervised learning.
Imitation learning is broader: inverse reinforcement learning infers a reward explanation, while adversarial imitation can match expert occupancy patterns without first recovering an explicit reward function.
The [GAIL paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.03476) makes the connection between occupancy matching, inverse RL, and adversarial training.

Reinforcement learning optimises expected return under an environment's dynamics and a reward specification.
For a discounted setting, the objective is

$$
  J(\pi)=\mathbb E_\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=0}^{\infty}\gamma^t r_t\right].
$$

Here $r_t$ is the reward at step $t$, and the expectation is over trajectories generated by the policy and the environment dynamics.
The discount factor satisfies $0\leq\gamma<1$.

Value-based methods estimate returns to support action selection, policy-based methods optimise a parameterised policy, and actor–critic methods combine a policy with a learned value estimate.
Rewards do not guarantee good behaviour if they omit something important or cannot be reliably optimised.

In policy papers, an “explicit policy” often directly outputs action parameters, while an “implicit policy” can score candidate actions with an energy and use a separate optimisation or sampling step.
These terms describe a policy interface; they should not silently replace the [generative-model density terminology](../machine-learning/generative-models.qmd#generative-models).
[Diffusion Policy](../../literature-review/action/diffusion-policy.qmd) compares these formulations in its motivation.

## What is online or offline? {#online-and-offline}

Online processing updates a result as observations arrive, using only information available so far.
Offline processing works on an already collected dataset or sequence.
An offline computation can still enforce causal masks and avoid future information at individual positions.

In RL, offline learning means learning from a fixed dataset without collecting new transitions during training; online learning includes interaction to obtain new experience.
“Online inference” and “online parameter learning” are separate claims.
The [state-space note](../machine-learning/state-space-models.qmd) shows how one model can support both batch sequence evaluation and incremental inference.

## Read the claim precisely {#questions}

| Question | Distinction to establish |
|---|---|
| When is the sequence available? | Incremental processing versus processing an already collected sequence. |
| Can a position read future inputs? | Causal access versus access to later observations. |
| Does training collect new experience? | Online interaction versus a fixed offline dataset. |
| Do parameters change during use? | Online parameter learning versus inference with fixed parameters. |

A system can answer these questions differently without contradiction.
Use [policies and reinforcement learning](policies.qmd) for the learning objective and [attention](../machine-learning/attention.qmd#projections) for causal masking.
